title: Frog — Digestive, Circulatory and Respiratory Systems
topicTitle: Frog: Blood vascular system (structure and working mechanism of heart); respiratory system (respiratory organs and physiology of respiration)

notes: Digestive system: mouth (tongue) → buccal cavity → oesophagus → stomach → intestine (small + large) → rectum → cloaca; liver and gall bladder; pancreas; bile for fat digestion.

**Frog digestive system — organs and secretions classified**

| Organ | Structure | Secretion / function |
|---|---|---|
| Tongue | Attached at FRONT, flips out to catch prey | Sticky saliva traps insects |
| Stomach | Broad, curved; pyloric valve at exit | HCl + pepsin — protein digestion |
| Liver + gall bladder | Three-lobed liver; bile stored in gall bladder | Bile emulsifies fat (no enzymes) |
| Pancreas | Irregular gland near duodenum | Amylase, lipase, trypsin — completes digestion |
| Small intestine | Long coiled tube; internal folds | Absorption of nutrients |
| Large intestine + cloaca | Short; cloaca is a shared exit | Water absorption; urine + gametes also exit here |
Circulatory system: 3-chambered heart (2 atria + 1 ventricle) → double circulation; oxygenated + deoxygenated blood partially mixed in the ventricle; systemic + pulmonary circuits.

Heart structure: right atrium (deoxygenated from body), left atrium (oxygenated from lungs/skin), single ventricle (partially mixed blood); ventricle has a spongy myocardium (crista ventriculi) that reduces mixing.
Respiratory system: lungs (pulmonary), moist skin (cutaneous), buccal cavity (buccal); tadpoles use gills.

**Frog respiration — three surfaces, one animal**

| Mode | Surface | When used | Share of gas exchange |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cutaneous | Moist naked skin | In water and at rest on land | Majority at rest — always working |
| Buccopharyngeal | Mouth-cavity lining | Shallow breathing at rest | Minor share |
| Pulmonary | Simple sac-like lungs | On land, active, in air | Dominant during activity |
| Larval (tadpole) | Gills (internal, then external) | Aquatic larval stage only | Lost at metamorphosis |

Physiology of respiration: inhalation (buccal floor lowers → air enters through nostrils), exhalation (buccal floor rises → air pushed into lungs); skin respiration is significant in water and at night.
Working mechanism of the heart: atria contract first (fill ventricle), then ventricle contracts (pump blood to lungs + body); valves (atrioventricular, conus valves) prevent backflow.

NEB focus: digestive system, blood vascular system (heart structure + working), respiratory system (organs + physiology).

### Extra depth — the working mechanism of the frog heart
Deoxygenated blood from body veins collects in the **sinus venosus** and enters the right atrium; oxygenated blood from the lungs enters the left atrium via pulmonary veins. Both atria contract nearly together, pushing blood through the common sino-atrial aperture into the **single ventricle**; a spiral valve in the **truncus arteriosus** then routes the streams: carotid arches (head), systemic arches (body), pulmocutaneous arches (lungs + skin). Because the ventricle mixes the two streams, organs receive partially oxygenated blood — the classic 'incomplete double circulation'. The heartbeat is **myogenic** (originates in the sinus venosus muscle, pace ≈ 40/min at rest); the heart continues beating briefly outside the body — a classic NEB demonstration.

### Extra depth — respiration in three modes
**Cutaneous** (skin, always, ~most of resting uptake): the moist, vascular skin diffuses O₂ in and CO₂ out — why the frog must stay damp. **Buccopharyngeal** (lining of mouth cavity): the floor rhythmically lowers and raises, drawing air in and out while nostrils close — the mouth acts as a force pump. **Pulmonary** (lungs, on land/active): nostrils open, floor lowers to draw air in, glottis opens, lungs fill by positive pressure (swallowing air — frogs lack a diaphragm); expiration is elastic recoil. Lungs are simple paired sacs with septa; no alveoli like mammals, so efficiency is lower — compensated by the skin.
confusion: The frog heart is 3-chambered (2 atria + 1 ventricle), NOT 4-chambered like mammals.
Blood is PARTIALLY MIXED in the frog ventricle (unlike the 4-chambered heart of birds and mammals where it is fully separated).
The spongy myocardium (crista ventriculi) in the frog ventricle helps reduce mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.
Frogs use THREE respiratory surfaces: lungs, moist skin (cutaneous), and the buccal cavity; tadpoles use gills.
The cloaca is the common exit for digestive, excretory, and reproductive systems.
Bile (from the liver, stored in the gall bladder) emulsifies fat in the small intestine; it is not a digestive enzyme.

exercises.question: Why is the frog heart called "partially mixed"? Explain the role of the spongy myocardium.
steps: One ventricle receives both oxygenated (left atrium) and deoxygenated (right atrium) blood
Blood mixes in the single ventricle
Spongy myocardium (crista ventriculi) forms ridges that direct blood, reducing mixing
exercises.answer: Because one ventricle mixes both types of blood; the spongy myocardium reduces (but does not eliminate) the mixing
